title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Anchorage, AK: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Anchorage, North Slope, pipeline and port construction inspectors: Part C choice, Part B in Alaska, cold-weather rules.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Anchorage: Six Days for North Slope, Pipeline, Port and Military Construction Inspectors
html:
Anchorage is where much of Alaska's industrial work is planned, staffed and supplied, even when the welding itself happens hundreds of miles away. Fabrication shops in the city build skids, pipe spools and truckable modules for the North Slope oil fields. The operator of the Trans Alaska Pipeline System keeps crews and contractors busy maintaining 800 miles of pipe, pump stations and the marine terminal at Valdez. On the city's own waterfront the Don Young Port of Alaska is replacing its cargo terminals, and at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson the Air Force is designing what The War Zone called one of its biggest military infrastructure projects. Each of those jobs needs welds inspected to a code, often in conditions most of the country never sees.

Atlantis NDT has a six-day course to prepare Alaskan candidates for the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) examination: welders and pipefitters moving into quality roles, shop and field QC inspectors, NDT technicians, and engineers working for owners and contractors. AWS writes the exam, administers it and issues the certificate, and each candidate deals with AWS directly, applying individually and meeting its experience and vision requirements in their own right. The course carries no AWS approval or endorsement, and Atlantis has not seen exam questions. There is no Atlantis classroom in Anchorage. Candidates can study the six days online at their own pace with an instructor available to answer questions, employers can host the six days at their shop or office for a group, and individuals can book one-to-one sessions online or in person at a location agreed when booking. The outline for each day is on the AWS CWI exam prep page.

Shops that build for the North Slope

Moving fabricated equipment to Prudhoe Bay, Kuparuk and the newer fields farther west is expensive, so producers use a mix of very large modules built outside the state and smaller truckable units, spools and skids that can travel the highways. Delta Constructors, an Anchorage oil field services company established in 2009, is one of the firms building that second kind. Its Anchorage shop has 42,000 square feet on five acres of shop and yard space and takes projects up to 21 feet wide and 100 tons; the company lists truckable modules up to 22 by 80 by 16 feet, fabricates carbon steel, stainless and duplex piping, manifolds and headers, and works to certified AWS and ASME welding procedures. Alaska Contractor magazine reported in summer 2026 that the company employed about 352 people in Alaska and that finding skilled workers was getting harder.

Shop work of this kind is where a CWI spends the day checking material certificates and heat numbers, confirming that each welder is qualified for the process, position and material, watching fit-up and preheat, measuring finished welds and making sure each spool and module leaves the yard with complete records. Production facility piping is usually specified to ASME B31.3 with Section IX qualifications, while the steel frames and pipe racks that carry it follow AWS D1.1.

The pipeline and the terminal at Valdez

Alyeska Pipeline Service Company operates the 800-mile Trans Alaska Pipeline System, which has moved about 18 billion barrels of oil since start-up in 1977. Keeping it running involves a continuing program of projects at pump stations, along the line and at the Valdez Marine Terminal. Alyeska's November 2025 update on terminal work described a crude tank that was emptied, cleaned, inspected, coated and given floor patch repairs, a buried section of crude piping examined for the first time since construction, a ballast water tank taken down and structures removed from a floating berth. Tank repairs, piping modifications and structural changes like these call for qualified welders and inspectors working to the operator's specifications and the relevant API and ASME standards.

Pipeline welding in Alaska follows API 1104, which the federal pipeline safety regulations incorporate by reference, so inspectors who choose API 1104 for Part C will recognize much of the exam's content from field work. Storage tank repair and alteration follow API 653; see API 653 for background.

The port, the base and public works in Anchorage

The Port of Alaska Modernization Program is replacing the city's aging cargo docks. In October 2026 KTUU reported that crews had spent the season driving large pilings into Cook Inlet for the new dock that will replace cargo terminal one, that progress fell short of goals after a late start and repeated stoppages in beluga whale protection zones, and that the port director still expected the terminal replacement to be finished in August 2028, with pile driving starting again early in 2027. Steel pipe piles and their splices, along with the wharf's structural steel and fittings, are welded work that is inspected against AWS D1.1 or the project's own specification.

At Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson the Air Force has a large program of new facilities in design. The War Zone reported in June 2026 that it covers hangars, squadron operations buildings and maintenance shops, corrosion control facilities, a munitions complex, petroleum operations facilities, housing and training centers, plus new taxiways, aprons and a runway extension, with timelines that depend on appropriations. Any funded part of that program will need structural, piping and fuel system welding and inspectors to match. State highway and bridge work adds a steady need for inspectors who know AWS D1.5.

Welding in the cold, and why the code book matters here

Alaska's climate turns code clauses that inspectors elsewhere rarely open into everyday business. AWS D1.1 sets an ambient temperature below which welding is not done unless the work area is enclosed and heated, and its preheat rules call for base metal below freezing to be warmed before welding even when the joint needs no other preheat. Wind, moisture and frost on the joint are all reasons a CWI can stop work. API 1104 and the ASME codes deal with weather and preheat mainly through the qualified procedure and general workmanship rules, which is one reason Alaskan inspectors learn to read welding procedure specifications closely: preheat, interpass temperature and any post-weld heat treatment have to be checked against the procedure rather than assumed.

On the exam, preheat, heat input, cooling rate, hydrogen cracking and the behavior of steel at low temperature come up in Part A as well as in the code books. Candidates who have welded through an Alaskan winter often find that material easier to picture than candidates from warmer states do.

Which book to take into Part C

AWS asks you to name one code for Part C when you apply. For Alaskan work the choice usually comes down to four of the books on the AWS application in November 2026:

  • API 1104, 22nd edition, for pipeline construction, tie-ins and repair, including gathering lines and the trans-Alaska system.
  • The ASME option, combining Section IX 2023 with B31.1 2024 and B31.3 2024, for production facilities, refineries, power plants and shop-built piping.
  • AWS D1.1:2020 for structural steel, the frames of modules and skids, port structures and buildings, including the military construction work at JBER.
  • AWS D1.5:2020 for highway bridges built for public owners such as the state transportation department.

Part C is open book, so the right choice is the code you will open at work for years afterwards. Further reading: API 1104, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 and AWS D1.5.

Taking the exam from Alaska

Parts A and C are computer-based tests delivered at Prometric sites; once AWS accepts your application, it sends the eligibility code you use to book them. Part B, the practical, is held only where AWS runs its CWI seminars. Anchorage was on the AWS list of CWI training locations in November 2026, so Alaskans do not always have to fly south for the practical, but a listed site is no promise of a session: the AWS Alaska Section posted that the seminar and Part B exam scheduled to begin on January 25, 2026 had been cancelled. Check the AWS seminar and exam schedule before you settle a study plan, and keep a fallback in mind, such as Sacramento, Los Angeles or Denver, the nearest sites in the lower 48 on the same list. AWS requires at least 72 percent on every part, so leave time for a retake.

Where Alaskans learn to weld: UAA and AVTEC

The University of Alaska Anchorage teaches welding within the Transportation and Power division of its Community and Technical College. It offers occupational endorsement certificates in Welding and Advanced Welding, a Nondestructive Testing endorsement that prepares students for entry-level work in welding and examination, and an Associate of Applied Science in Technology, and the department says it trains and tests students on the same weld tests that industry gives. In Seward, the state's Alaska Vocational Technical Center (AVTEC) runs a 1,110-hour Industrial Welding program that starts in January and August, covers stick, wire feed and TIG welding with an introduction to nondestructive testing, and sets its top achievement level at a structural certification to AWS unlimited thickness and a 6G pipe certification to ASME Section IX, with the testing done in Anchorage through Alaska Industrial X-Ray.

Both routes help a future CWI. Welding education reduces the years of experience AWS asks for, and a grounding in nondestructive testing makes the Part A questions on methods and their limitations far easier.

Studying on rotation

Many Alaskan candidates work two weeks on and two weeks off, or longer stints at remote camps where the connection is slow. The online format suits that pattern. Load up on reading before you fly out and work through the text-heavy topics, such as metallurgy, welding processes and safety, while on rotation, then save timed practice papers and your questions for the instructor for the weeks in town, when the connection is dependable. Code-book drills need only the book and a set of tabs, so they travel well.

For Part B, practise with gauges on real welds whenever you are at the shop: fillet weld gauges, an undercut gauge, a bridge cam gauge, a hi-lo gauge and calipers. The Practical NDT welding workshop lets you rehearse visual inspection steps in a browser, and the free NDT practice tests cover Part A's testing-methods content.

Six days at an Anchorage shop or office

A fabricator, pipeline contractor or engineering firm with several people preparing for the CWI can bring the six days to its own premises. The practical day can work on spools and module welds from the shop floor and on the company's own procedure and welder qualification records, and the code day can follow API 1104 for a pipeline group or the ASME option for a facilities shop. The employer picks the weeks, which in Alaska usually means fitting around the construction season, whether that is summer on the waterfront or winter on the Slope.

The CWI stays personal even when the course is shared. Each person applies to AWS in their own name, supplies their own vision form and experience records and sits every part of the exam individually.

Proving experience from camp and seasonal work

AWS weighs education against years of welding-related work. The scale runs from one year of experience with a bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding technology, through two with a relevant associate degree or higher, three with engineering or technical courses that count toward a welding bachelor's and four with completed trade or vocational courses, to five with a high school diploma or equivalent. Nine years are needed with eighth-grade schooling and twelve with less. AWS decides what qualifies, and the experience must be verifiable.

Seasonal and rotational careers can make that verification harder. Keep a record of each employer, camp or project, the dates and rotation pattern, the processes and materials you welded, the codes the work followed and any duties close to inspection, such as hydrotest preparation, weld mapping or checking fit-up. Ask supervisors to confirm the work while projects are fresh, because contractors on short Alaskan jobs move on quickly.

The vision test is recorded on the AWS visual acuity exam form by a qualified examiner, and the current form on aws.org sets the near-vision and color perception standard. AWS limits how old that test may be at exam time, so plan it around your application rather than relying on a routine eye exam from months earlier. The CWI requirements guide sets out the full rules.

After the CWI in Alaska

Alaskan CWIs often combine the credential with others. Many add nondestructive testing methods, which require training and certification by the employer under its written practice; Atlantis offers training based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, such as UT Level 2, MT Level 2 and VT Level 2, and the employer certifies the technician afterwards. Inspectors heading toward owner-side roles at production facilities and terminals look at API 510, 570 and 653; Atlantis offers self-paced API inspector exam preparation, with API administering those exams and issuing the certificates. The CWI itself runs for nine years, with renewals at the third and sixth and a choice at the ninth that includes retaking Part B or documenting 80 professional development hours.

Making an Anchorage enquiry

Tell us whether the course is for one person or a group, which format you want, which code book you plan to use for Part C and when you hope to sit the exam, including whether you are aiming for an Alaska Part B session or a lower-48 site. For a group at your shop, add the location and the weeks that fit your construction season. If you are unsure your experience qualifies, a few lines about your work history are enough for us to point out what to raise with AWS. Fees are quoted on request. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can I take Part B in Anchorage?
faq.a: Possibly. Anchorage was on the AWS list of CWI training locations in November 2026, but a listing is no promise of a session, and the AWS Alaska Section reported that one scheduled to begin on January 25, 2026 was cancelled. Check the AWS schedule and keep a lower-48 site as a fallback.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section in Alaska?
faq.a: Yes. AWS lists the Alaska Section as Section 125 in District 19. Its announcements, including notices about CWI seminars and Part B sessions in the state, are posted on its page at sections.aws.org.

faq.q: Which code book should a North Slope facilities inspector choose?
faq.a: Usually the ASME option, because production facility piping is normally built to ASME B31.3 with Section IX qualifications. Inspectors who mostly see module steel and pipe racks may prefer AWS D1.1, and pipeline inspectors API 1104.

faq.q: Does cold-weather welding come up on the CWI exam?
faq.a: Preheat, cooling rate, hydrogen cracking and the behavior of steel at low temperature are part of the fundamentals, and AWS D1.1 has explicit rules on ambient temperature and cold base metal. Field experience in Alaska helps with those questions.

faq.q: Can I prepare during a two-week rotation?
faq.a: Yes. The online format is self-paced with no fixed class times, so you can read on rotation and use your weeks in town for timed practice papers and questions to the instructor.

faq.q: Do UAA or AVTEC graduates need less experience before applying?
faq.a: Welding education reduces what AWS asks for: completed trade or vocational courses bring the requirement to four years, and an associate degree or higher in a qualifying field brings it to two. AWS classes each program, so submit your records with the application.

faq.q: Can an Anchorage fabricator host the course for its QC staff?
faq.a: Yes. The corporate format delivers the six days at the employer's shop or office, using its own spools, module welds and qualification records, in weeks that fit around the construction season.

faq.q: Will Atlantis issue my CWI certificate?
faq.a: No. AWS administers every part of the examination and issues the certification. Atlantis prepares candidates and has no role in the exam itself, and it is not approved or endorsed by AWS.

faq.q: How do I request a quote from Alaska?
faq.a: Use the enquiry link on this page with the format, the number of people, your Part C code and your target exam period. Fees are quoted on request, and Atlantis answers within one business day.
